# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

#### fn [kill_child_storage](https://docs.rs#tymethod.kill_child_storage)(

    child_info: &[ChildInfo](https://docs.rs/sp-storage/25.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sp_storage/enum.ChildInfo.html),
    maybe_limit: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)>,
    maybe_cursor: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<&[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]>,
) -> [MultiRemovalResults](https://docs.rs/struct.MultiRemovalResults.html)

Clear an entire child storage.

Deletes all keys from the overlay and up to `maybe_limit` keys from the backend. No
limit is applied if `maybe_limit` is `None`. Returns the cursor for the next call as `Some`
if the child trie deletion operation is incomplete. In this case, it should be passed into
the next call to avoid unaccounted iterations on the backend. Returns also the the number
of keys that were removed from the backend, the number of unique keys removed in total
(including from the overlay) and the number of backend iterations done.

As long as `maybe_cursor` is passed from the result of the previous call, then the number of
iterations done will only ever be one more than the number of keys removed.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

An implementation is free to delete more keys than the specified limit as long as it is able to do that in constant time.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sp_externalities/lib.rs.html#227)

#### fn [storage_start_transaction](https://docs.rs#tymethod.storage_start_transaction)(&mut self)

Start a new nested transaction.

This allows to either commit or roll back all changes made after this call to the
top changes or the default child changes. For every transaction there cam be a
matching call to either `storage_rollback_transaction` or `storage_commit_transaction`.
Any transactions that are still open after returning from runtime are committed
automatically.

Changes made without any open transaction are committed immediately.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/sp_externalities/lib.rs.html#233)#### fn [storage_rollback_transaction](https://docs.rs#tymethod.storage_rollback_transaction)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

# meerkat - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/meerkat/0.7.12/meerkat/

## Expand description

Meerkat - Rust Agentic Interface Kit

A minimal, high-performance agent harness for LLM-powered applications.

[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

All production surfaces (CLI, REST, RPC, MCP) use the **runtime-backed** path:
`SessionService` (substrate) + `MeerkatMachine` (control plane).
The runtime owns keep-alive, Queue/Steer routing, comms drain, and ingress.

`build_ephemeral_service` is available for **testing and embedded use** where
runtime semantics (keep-alive, Steer, comms-driven admission) are not needed.
It supports Queue-only turns and will reject Steer/render_metadata.

For the runtime-backed entry point, see [`meerkat_rpc::SessionRuntime`] or
the REST/MCP server crates.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [meerkat_contracts](https://docs.rs/meerkat-contracts/0.7.12/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/meerkat_contracts/index.html)as contracts;

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [help](https://docs.rs/help/index.html)
- Shared helpers for dedicated Meerkat help surfaces.
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Prelude module for convenient imports
- [session_](https://docs.rs/session_runtime/index.html)- runtime
- Surface-agnostic session runtime — the canonical orchestrator that
glues `PersistentSessionService`,`StagedSessionRegistry`,`MeerkatMachine`, and the optional`LiveAdapterHost`together.
- [surface](https://docs.rs/surface/index.html)
- Shared surface infrastructure helpers.

# sim_lib_sound_timbre - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-sound-timbre/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_sound_timbre/

## Expand description

Timbre models and spectral filters for the SIM music constellation.

This crate defines the [ Timbre](https://docs.rs/struct.Timbre.html) type – a named synthesis recipe with a
default envelope, descriptive metadata, and a filter chain – the

[synthesis methods (pure sine, sawtooth, square, triangle, organ pipe, Karplus-Strong, FM, and inharmonic bell), the spectral](https://docs.rs/enum.TimbreRecipe.html)

`TimbreRecipe`[family, and a runtime surface that installs the built-in timbre cards as a SIM lib.](https://docs.rs/enum.Filter.html)

`Filter`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Sound](https://docs.rs/struct.SoundTimbreLib.html)- Timbre - Lib
- Host-registered lib exporting the built-in timbre cards and registry, built
on the shared `SurfacePackLib`
- [Timbre](https://docs.rs/struct.Timbre.html)
- A named instrument timbre: a synthesis recipe plus a default envelope, descriptive metadata, and a post-synthesis filter chain.
- [Timbre](https://docs.rs/struct.TimbreMeta.html)- Meta
- Descriptive metadata characterizing a `Timbre`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Attack](https://docs.rs/enum.AttackKind.html)- Kind
- The character of a timbre’s onset.
- [Filter](https://docs.rs/enum.Filter.html)
- A spectral filter applied to a tone’s partials.
- [Timbre](https://docs.rs/enum.TimbreRecipe.html)- Recipe
- A synthesis recipe describing how to build the partials of a tone.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [bell_](https://docs.rs/fn.bell_inharmonic.html)- inharmonic
- Returns an inharmonic bell timbre from the given partial ratios.
- [fm_pair](https://docs.rs/fn.fm_pair.html)
- Returns a two-operator FM timbre with the given modulator ratio and index.
- [install_](https://docs.rs/fn.install_sound_timbre_lib.html)- sound_ - timbre_ - lib
- Installs the sound-timbre lib into `cx`, registering the built-in timbre cards and the timbre registry export records (idempotent).
- [karplus_](https://docs.rs/fn.karplus_strong.html)- strong
- Returns a Karplus-Strong plucked-string timbre with the given damping.
- [organ_](https://docs.rs/fn.organ_pipe.html)- pipe
- Returns an organ-pipe timbre blending the given harmonic stops.
- [pure_](https://docs.rs/fn.pure_sine.html)- sine
- Returns a pure-sine timbre.
- [sawtooth](https://docs.rs/fn.sawtooth.html)
- Returns a sawtooth timbre with the given number of harmonics.
- [square](https://docs.rs/fn.square.html)
- Returns a square-wave timbre with the given number of harmonics.
- [triangle](https://docs.rs/fn.triangle.html)
- Returns a triangle-wave timbre with the given number of harmonics.

# meerkat_client - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/meerkat-client/0.7.12/meerkat_client/

## Expand description

meerkat-client — shim re-exports.

The LLM wire-client trait + plumbing moved to `meerkat-llm-core`;
per-provider clients (`AnthropicClient`, `OpenAiClient`, `GeminiClient`,
`OpenAiLiveClient`, `OpenAiCompatibleClient`)
moved to `meerkat-anthropic`, `meerkat-openai`, `meerkat-gemini`.
Provider-runtime types moved to `meerkat-core::provider_runtime`.
Auth primitives moved to `meerkat-auth-core`.

This crate is retained as a thin shim so that downstream
`meerkat_client::*` imports continue to work without an import sweep.
B2 split (2026-04-18).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

# npcsh 1.2.32 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/npcsh/1.2.32

`npcsh` makes the most of LLMs and agents through slash commands and interactive modes, all from the command line. Build teams of agents, schedule them on jobs, engineer context, and design custom Jinja Execution templates (Jinxes) for you and your agents to invoke.

To get started, view the latest release in the sidebar on github, and download the executable binary for your system. Once downloaded, ensure that it is executable.

```
#linux
```
Then run the executable

```
```
Alternatively, you can install with brew or pip.

```
```
```
pip install 'npcsh[lite]'
```
Once installed, run `npcsh` to enter the NPC shell. Also provides the CLI tools `npc` and `npcsh-bench`.

`.npc` files are directly executable with shebangs (`#!/usr/bin/env npc`):

## Benchmark Results

How well can a model drive `npcsh` as an agentic shell? 125 tasks across 15 categories — from basic shell commands to multi-step workflows, code debugging, and tool chaining — scored pass/fail. Comparisons with other agent coders coming soon. For a more comprehensive view of npcsh's capabilities and the advantages of the NPC Context-Agent-Tool data layer, check out [ALARA for Agents: Least-Privilege Context Engineering Through Portable Composable Multi-Agent Teams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.20380)

```
```
## Usage

-
Get help with a task:
-
Edit files:
-
**Search & Knowledge**
-
**Computer Use**
-
**Multi-Agent Discussions**

## Agent Formats

npcsh supports multiple ways to define agents inside your `npc_team/` directory. You can mix all three formats — `.npc` files take precedence if names collide.

** .npc files** — Full-featured YAML agent definitions with model, provider, jinxes, and more:

```
#!/usr/bin/env npc
name: analyst
primary_directive: You analyze data and provide insights.
model: qwen3:8b
provider: ollama
jinxes:
  - skills/data-analysis
```
** agents.md** — Define multiple agents in a single markdown file. Each

`## heading` = agent name, body = directive:```
You summarize long documents into concise bullet points.
You verify claims against reliable sources and flag inaccuracies.
```
** agents/ directory** — One

`.md` file per agent. Filename (minus `.md`) = agent name. Supports YAML frontmatter:```
model: gemini-2.5-flash
provider: gemini
You translate content between languages while preserving tone and idiom.
```
All three formats are supported by both the **Python** and **Rust** editions of npcsh. Agents from `agents.md` and `agents/` inherit the team's default model/provider from `team.ctx`.

The full team structure:

```
npc_team/
├── team.ctx           # Team config (model, provider, forenpc, context)
├── coordinator.npc    # YAML agent definitions
├── analyst.npc
├── agents.md          # Markdown-defined agents
├── agents/            # One .md file per agent
│   └── translator.md
├── jinxes/            # Workflows and tools
│   ├── research.jinx
│   └── skills/        # Knowledge-content skills
└── tools/             # Custom tool functions
```
This means you can bring agents from other ecosystems — if you already have an `agents.md` or an `agents/` directory from Claude Code, Codex, Amp, or any other tool, just drop them into your `npc_team/` and npcsh will pick them up alongside your `.npc` files.

## Launching AI Coding Tools with NPC Teams

Your `npc_team/` works beyond `npcsh` — you can launch any major AI coding tool as an NPC from your team using the CLI launchers from [npcpy](https://github.com/cagostino/npcpy). Each tool gets the NPC's persona injected and gains awareness of the other team members.

```
# Launch Claude Code as an NPC (interactive picker)
# Launch as a specific NPC
# Same for other coding tools
# Point to a specific team directory
```
The launcher discovers your team from `./npc_team` or `~/.npcsh/npc_team`, lets you pick an NPC, and starts the tool with that NPC's directive. For Claude Code, it also passes the other NPCs as sub-agents via `--agents`.

For deeper integration (jinxes exposed as MCP tools, team switching mid-conversation), register the NPC plugin:

meerkat-tools - Tool validation and dispatch for Meerkat

[to combine built-in tools with external MCP tools.](https://docs.rs/builtin/composite/struct.CompositeDispatcher.html)

`CompositeDispatcher````
use meerkat_tools::{
    CompositeDispatcher, BuiltinToolConfig, FileTaskStore,
    find_project_root, ensure_rkat_dir,
};
let project_root = find_project_root(&std::env::current_dir().unwrap())
    .expect("no .rkat directory found");
ensure_rkat_dir(&project_root).unwrap();
let store = Arc::new(FileTaskStore::in_project(&project_root));
let dispatcher = CompositeDispatcher::new(
    store,
    &BuiltinToolConfig::default(),
    Some(project_root),
    None,
    None,
    None,
)?;
```

# precise - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/precise/0.1.11/precise/

## Expand description

Decimal representation of the single rational number whose value is mathematically equal to the input float.

Note that this is almost never an appropriate way to print user-facing
values. For that, use the [ryu](https://github.com/dtolnay/ryu) crate instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
fn main() {
    // 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625
    println!("{}", precise::to_string(0.1));
}
```

# rill_core_model - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rill-core-model/0.5.0-beta.7/rill_core_model/

## Expand description

Wave Digital Filter (WDF) core and physical modeling — elements, adapters, analysis, and resonant models for analog circuit and acoustic simulation.

All types are generic over [ rill_core::Transcendental](https://docs.rs/trait.Transcendental.html), supporting both

`f32`
and `f64`. SIMD-accelerated batch processing is available via
`process_incident_vector` methods on [,](https://docs.rs/struct.Resistor.html)

`Resistor`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Capacitor.html)

`Capacitor`[, and](https://docs.rs/struct.Inductor.html)

`Inductor`[, plus the free function [](https://docs.rs/struct.Diode.html)

`Diode``elements::process_batch_simd`].[§](https://docs.rs#modules)Modules

- `macros`— WDF eDSL macros for defining elements and filters
- `analysis`— frequency response and distortion analysis
- `constants`— physical constants and tolerances
- `wdf`— WDF-based filter models
- `string`— 1D waveguide string models with stiffness and damping
- `plate`— 2D FDTD waveguide mesh for plates and membranes
- `modal`— modal synthesis via parallel resonant filter banks
- `cavity`— Helmholtz cavity resonators and coupled cavity arrays

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

WDF elements are built around the [ WdfElement](https://docs.rs/trait.WdfElement.html) trait, which defines a
port resistance, wave processing, and state update cycle. Elements can be
combined via

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.SeriesAdapter.html)

`SeriesAdapter`[to form arbitrary linear circuits. Nonlinear elements like](https://docs.rs/struct.ParallelAdapter.html)

`ParallelAdapter`[use Newton-Raphson iteration for implicit solution.](https://docs.rs/struct.Diode.html)

`Diode`References:

- A. Fettweis, “Wave Digital Filters: Theory and Practice” (1986)
- K. J. Werner et al., “An Improved and Generalized Diode Clipper Model for Wave Digital Filters” (2015)

# rill_core_actor - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rill-core-actor/0.5.0-beta.7/rill_core_actor/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rill-core-actor--actor-model-infrastructure)Rill Core Actor — actor model infrastructure

A lightweight, domain-agnostic actor model for lock-free message passing. Actors are single-threaded: handler is created and drained on the same thread.

[§](https://docs.rs#key-types)Key types

| Type | Role |
|---|---|
| `Actor<M>` | Handler + mailbox — drained in-place (no separate thread) |
| `ActorRef<M>` | Thread-safe handle to send messages to an actor |
| `ActorSystem` | Named actor registry, dead letters, `spawn()`,`spawn_detached()` |

[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

```
// Handler drained inline (Graph, Rack):
system.spawn(name, handler) → Actor<M> → actor.drain() on caller's thread
// Handler created & drained inside a new thread (Servo, factory modules):
system.spawn_detached(name, make_handler, ms) → ActorRef<M>
  └── thread::spawn: handler = make_handler() → actor.drain() loop
```

# moorage 0.0.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/moorage/0.0.1

# moorage

Install your self-authored agent **skills and plugins** into one central home, and
wire every agent harness to them from a single source of truth. A small Rust CLI.

*(Renamed from  skilldock, which collided on GitHub.)*

## Commands

```
moorage install   SOURCE [--mode dev|normal] [--skills a,b] [--harnesses claude,pi,omp,codex]
                         [--force] [--dry-run] [--no-post-install]
moorage uninstall NAME... [--dry-run]
moorage update    NAME... [--force] [--dry-run]
moorage list
moorage doctor    [--json]
```
All commands accept the six root overrides (see *Roots* below). `--dry-run` prints the
full action plan — skills, links, hook placements, registration merges, backups,
post_install — and mutates nothing.

## Skills (no manifest — behavior unchanged)

`SOURCE` may be a directory containing `SKILL.md` (single skill) or a repo with
`skills/*/SKILL.md` (multi-skill; scanned one level). The skill **name** comes from
the `SKILL.md` frontmatter `name:` and must be lowercase `[a-z0-9-]`, ≤ 64 chars,
with a non-empty `description:` (pi's discovery rule — enforced so the link name is
correct). A `skills/*` layout is **preferred** over a repo-root `SKILL.md`, so a repo
carrying both installs its `skills/<name>` payloads (the baseline shape).

Each skill installs to `~/.moorage/skills/{name}`:

| Mode | `~/.moorage/skills/{name}`is | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| `dev`(default) | a symlink to the repo payload | authoring / iterating |
| `normal`(alias:`local`) | a real copy (excludes `.git`,`__pycache__`) | pinned snapshot |

and the agent roots link into the home:

```
~/.agents/skills/{name}  --+                              +-- dev:    repo payload (live)
                           +-->  ~/.moorage/skills/{name} -+
~/.claude/skills/{name}  --+                              +-- normal: a copy in the home
```
oh-my-pi reads both locations; all agents dedupe by real path.

## Plugins (`moorage.toml` manifest)

A `moorage.toml` at the repo root (or passed directly as `SOURCE`) upgrades a repo to
a plugin. **Its absence changes nothing** — no-manifest repos keep the exact behavior
above.

```
 = "conversate"          # optional plugin label (names placed hook files)
[]                    # optional preferences (see Precedence)
 = "dev"                 # dev | normal | local
 = ["claude", "pi", "omp", "codex"]
[[]]
 = "."                   # payload dir, repo-root-relative ("." = repo root)
 = "normal"              # optional per-skill override
 = ["claude"]       # optional per-skill override
[[]]
 = "hooks/claude/settings-snippet.json"   # merged into <claude-root>/settings.json
[[]]
 = "hooks/pi/conv-turn-counter.ts"         # placed into <pi-root>/agent/extensions/
[[]]
 = "hooks/pi/conv-turn-counter.ts"         # placed into <omp-root>/hooks/{stage}/
 = "pre"                                    # default "pre" when omitted
[[]]
 = "hooks/codex/hooks.json"                # merged into <codex-root>/hooks.json
[]
 = ["python scripts/example.py init"]         # optional; cwd = canonical skill dir
```
### Preference precedence

`CLI flags > per-skill entry > [install] table > built-in defaults` (mode `dev`, all
four harnesses). `--mode` / `--harnesses` on the command line mean "override the
manifest". The `harnesses` list gates both the skill links (`claude` → claude-root
link; any of `pi`/`omp`/`codex` → agents-root link) and the hook wiring per harness.
Per-skill `harnesses` gate that skill's links; plugin-level hooks follow
`CLI > [install] > default`.

### Hook FILES (pi, omp)

Placed as **file symlinks** named `moorage-{label}-{basename}` (label = manifest
`name`, else the first skill's name) pointing at the canonical copy inside
`~/.moorage/skills/{name}/...` — so dev/normal switching is transparent. If file
symlinks are unavailable (Windows without Developer Mode) the file is **copied** with
a loud warning, and doctor tracks drift of copied placements. Junctions are dir-only
and hardlinks die across volumes, so neither is used for files. Hook scripts must
live inside a `[[skills]]` payload (otherwise no canonical home copy exists — the
install refuses that hook).

### Registration MERGES (claude, codex)

The snippet's `hooks` block merges into the target config via a serde_json
round-trip that preserves unrelated keys:

- claude → `<claude-root>/settings.json`
- codex → `<codex-root>/hooks.json`(plus a printed reminder that codex loads hooks only with`[features] hooks = true`in`~/.codex/config.toml`— moorage**never**edits that file)

Merges are **append-if-absent** (exact-equality dedupe ⇒ idempotent re-installs), and
a syntactically invalid target config is refused, never clobbered. Before the
**first** modification of each config, a `.bak` copy goes into `~/.moorage/backups/`
(named `{basename}.{epoch}.bak`, recorded in state).

**Command-path rewriting** (design ruling; the v2 exact rule is unrecovered): every
whitespace-separated token of a `command` / `commandWindows` string that resolves —
relative to an installed skill payload root — to an existing file is rewritten to the
absolute path of that file under the canonical home
(`~/.moorage/skills/{name}/...`). The **home** path, never the source repo path, so
dev-mode symlinks keep the loop live. Rewritten paths containing spaces are quoted; a
token that itself contains spaces can never match (whitespace split — a known v2
limitation). Snippets should therefore reference their scripts by payload-relative
paths (e.g. `hooks/claude/counter.ps1`).

### Reversibility

Every inserted JSON entry is persisted **verbatim** in `state.toml` *and* is
self-marked by containing the `~/.moorage/skills/{name}` path in its command (no
marker keys are injected — that would fight harness schema validation). `uninstall`:

- unmerges exactly the recorded entries (falling back to the home-path marker for
entries a user edited in place); emptied configs are left as `{}`, never deleted;
- removes placed hook files and agent links (links are dropped, targets untouched);
- removes the home entry — for dev mode the **symlink only**, never the target repo;
- deletes the state record.

Source repositories are never touched. Legacy state records (pre-plugin, five fields)
still load; uninstalling one derives the two conventional agent-link paths and
deletes each **only after verifying it actually points into the moorage home** —
anything else is skipped with a warning.

### post_install

Commands run after all components are placed, with `cwd` = the canonical skill dir in
the home (first skill for multi-skill plugins). Each command is echoed and its
outcome recorded in state. `--no-post-install` skips them (recorded as `skipped`). A
failing command **reports loudly, marks the state record ( failed(N)), sets exit
code 1, and does NOT roll back the install** (design ruling — fix the cause and
re-run, or uninstall).

`update` never runs post_install.## update

- **dev**installs: verify and repair the whole chain — home link, agent links, hook files; re-apply merges when snippets changed (stale recorded entries are unmerged, new ones merged; stale hook files removed).
- **normal**installs: hash-compare (in-crate FNV-1a-64 over the payload tree) and re-copy- **only if the source changed**;- **refuse**when the installed copy was hand-edited (or when a legacy record has no stored hash to verify against) —- `--force`overrides.

## doctor

Read-only, always. Checks: state.toml parse health; full chain integrity (agent link
→ home → payload); dangling/re-targeted links; placed hook files (missing, dangling,
copy drift vs canonical); merged registrations (recorded entries still present,
target configs valid); **orphaned** moorage-marked entries (home path in the command
but absent from state); unmanaged entries (reported, never touched) incl. pi
name-rule violations; shadowing (same name under claude-root and agents-root
resolving to different real paths); normal-mode content drift vs source; dev-mode git
hygiene (dirty tree, non-main branch — best effort); manifest preference drift
(manifest prefers a different mode than installed); `AGENTS.md` inside a skill dir
(pi issue #2473). `--json` emits the findings machine-readably. Exit code is 0 even
with findings; nonzero means doctor itself failed to run.

## Conflicts, idempotency, dry-run

- An entry already resolving to the right target is left alone (idempotent re-runs); merges dedupe by exact equality.
- A conflicting foreign entry is **refused**with a clear message;`--force`renames it to a sibling`{name}.bak-N`and replaces it.
- `--dry-run`prints the full plan and changes nothing (configs are only read).

## Roots (for tests / alternate setups)

Flag > env > default, uniformly:

| Setting | Flag | Env | Default | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| home | `--home` | `MOORAGE_HOME` | `~/.moorage` | canonical home, state, backups |
| agents root | `--agents-root` | `MOORAGE_AGENTS_ROOT` | `~/.agents` | pi/omp/codex skill links |
| claude root | `--claude-root` | `MOORAGE_CLAUDE_ROOT` | `~/.claude` | Claude skill links + `settings.json`merges |
| pi root | `--pi-root` | `MOORAGE_PI_ROOT` | `~/.pi` | hook files under `agent/extensions/` |
| omp root | `--omp-root` | `MOORAGE_OMP_ROOT` | `~/.omp` | hook files under `hooks/{stage}/` |
| codex root | `--codex-root` | `MOORAGE_CODEX_ROOT` | `~/.codex` | `hooks.json`merges |

## state.toml

`~/.moorage/state.toml` records, per skill: `name`, `mode`, `source`, `installed`/
`updated` (epoch secs), and — for plugin installs — `plugin` label, `manifest` path,
effective `harnesses`, `home_kind` (symlink/junction/copy), `copy_hash` (normal
mode), `[[links]]` (path/kind/target), `[[hook_files]]` (path/kind/target),
`[[merges]]` (file/event/verbatim entry), `[[post_install]]` (command/status), and
`[[backups]]` (original/backup). Legacy five-field records load unchanged.

## Windows link fallback

Directory links try: real symlink (needs Developer Mode or elevation) → NTFS
**junction** via `cmd /c mklink /J` (no privileges) → **copy** with a loud warning.
File placements try: file symlink → copy (drift tracked by doctor). On non-Windows,
symlinks are used directly.

## Unverified upstream paths (honesty notes)

- **omp**: upstream documents only- *project-level*- `.omp/hooks/{stage}/*.ts`discovery. The user-level- `<omp-root>/hooks/{stage}/`placement is a- **best-documented-guess**(unverified upstream). doctor emits a- `warn`note when omp hook files are installed; override with- `--omp-root`.
- **codex**: whether codex reads a- *user-level*- `hooks.json`at all is- **unverified**(only project-level- `.codex/hooks.json`is documented). doctor emits a- `warn`note when codex merges are installed; override with- `--codex-root`.
- **pi**(- `~/.pi/agent/extensions`) and- **claude**(- `~/.claude/settings.json`) are documented/known paths.

## Design rulings (unrecovered v2 details, decided here)

- **Command rewriting token rule**: whitespace token → resolve against installed payload roots (manifest order, first match) → rewrite to the absolute canonical home path; quote only when the result contains spaces; absolute tokens skipped.
- **Mode name**: the CLI keeps- `dev|normal`;- `local`(the v2 name) is accepted as an alias both on the CLI and in manifests.
- **omp**:- `stage`default- `"pre"`(the only value ever observed).
- **post_install failure**: loud warning +- `failed(N)`in state + exit 1, no rollback;- `--no-post-install`records- `skipped`;- `update`never runs post_install.
- `--force`backups- `{name}.bak-N`convention (the pinned minimal-Rust behavior) instead of moving into- `~/.moorage/backups/`; the backups dir holds config- `.bak`snapshots only, named- `{basename}.{epoch}.bak`.
- **backups/ contents are permanent**: uninstall does not delete taken backups (traceability).
- **Multi-skill plugins**: post_install cwd = first skill's canonical dir; hook artifacts are named after the manifest- `name`(else the first skill); the plugin component ledger (hook files, merges, post_install, backups) rides on the first skill's state record.
- **Manifests must declare**: a manifest with no skills entry is an error (hooks need a payload to live in).- `[[skills]]`
- **Corrupt state.toml**: mutating commands refuse to run over an unparseable ledger (protecting the live records); doctor reports it as a- `fail`finding.
- `update`flags- `--force`(attested) plus- `--dry-run`(inferred-carried).
- **Content hashing**: in-crate FNV-1a-64 (stable across releases, zero deps) — std's- `DefaultHasher`is explicitly not used for persisted hashes.

## Build

```
cargo build --release          # binary at target/release/moorage(.exe)
cargo install --path .         # optional: install to ~/.cargo/bin
```
Tests: `cargo test` (unit: manifest parse, merge/unmerge/rewrite, state round-trip
incl. legacy records) and `python -m pytest tests/ -q` (29 black-box tests against
the built binary with all six roots pinned to temp dirs; set `MOORAGE_BIN` to point
at a specific exe, else `target/debug/moorage`).

Requires a stable Rust toolchain. Dependencies: `clap` (CLI), `serde` + `toml`
(manifests + state), `serde_json` (registration merges).

# polkadot_jemalloc_shim - Rust

## Expand description

Shim crate to enable `jemalloc-allocator` feature for Polkadot crates.

Because [there doesn’t exist any easier way right now](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/1197), we
need an entire crate to handle `jemalloc` enabling/disabling. This way we can enable it by

# sp_io - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sp-io/48.0.0/target-redirect/sp_io/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#substrate-primitives-io)Substrate Primitives: IO

This crate contains interfaces for the runtime to communicate with the outside world, ergo `io`.
In other context, such interfaces are referred to as “**host functions**”.

Each set of host functions are defined with an instance of the
[ sp_runtime_interface::runtime_interface](https://docs.rs/sp-runtime-interface-proc-macro/21.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sp_runtime_interface_proc_macro/attr.runtime_interface.html) macro.

Most notably, this crate contains host functions for:

All of the default host functions provided by this crate, and by default contained in all
substrate-based clients are amalgamated in [ SubstrateHostFunctions](https://docs.rs/type.SubstrateHostFunctions.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#externalities)Externalities

Host functions go hand in hand with the concept of externalities. Externalities are an environment in which host functions are provided, and thus can be accessed. Some host functions are only accessible in an externality environment that provides it.

A typical error for substrate developers is the following:

This code will panic with the following error:

`thread 'main' panicked at '`get_version_1` called outside of an Externalities-provided environment.'`Such error messages should always be interpreted as “code accessing host functions accessed outside of externalities”.

An externality is any type that implements [ sp_externalities::Externalities](https://docs.rs/sp-externalities/0.34.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sp_externalities/trait.Externalities.html). A simple example
of which is

[, which is commonly used in tests and is exported from this crate.](https://docs.rs/type.TestExternalities.html)

`TestExternalities````
use sp_io::{storage::get, TestExternalities};
TestExternalities::default().execute_with(|| {
	let data = get(b"hello world");
});
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [allocator](https://docs.rs/allocator/index.html)
- Wasm only interface that provides functions for calling into the allocator.
- [crypto](https://docs.rs/crypto/index.html)
- Interfaces for working with crypto related types from within the runtime.
- [default_](https://docs.rs/default_child_storage/index.html)- child_ - storage
- Interface for accessing the child storage for default child trie, from within the runtime.
- [hashing](https://docs.rs/hashing/index.html)
- Interface that provides functions for hashing with different algorithms.
- [logging](https://docs.rs/logging/index.html)
- Interface that provides functions for logging from within the runtime.
- [misc](https://docs.rs/misc/index.html)
- Interface that provides miscellaneous functions for communicating between the runtime and the node.
- [offchain](https://docs.rs/offchain/index.html)
- Interface that provides functions to access the offchain functionality.
- [offchain_](https://docs.rs/offchain_index/index.html)- index
- Interface that provides functions to access the Offchain DB.
- [panic_](https://docs.rs/panic_handler/index.html)- handler
- WASM-only interface which allows for aborting the execution in case of an unrecoverable error.
- [storage](https://docs.rs/storage/index.html)
- Interface for accessing the storage from within the runtime.
- [transaction_](https://docs.rs/transaction_index/index.html)- index
- Interface that provides transaction indexing API.
- [trie](https://docs.rs/trie/index.html)
- Interface that provides trie related functionality.
- [wasm_](https://docs.rs/wasm_tracing/index.html)- tracing
- Interface to provide tracing facilities for wasm. Modelled after tokios `tracing`-crate interfaces. See`sp-tracing`for more information.

# sp_io - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sp-io/48.0.0/sp_io/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#substrate-primitives-io)Substrate Primitives: IO

This crate contains interfaces for the runtime to communicate with the outside world, ergo `io`.
In other context, such interfaces are referred to as “**host functions**”.

Each set of host functions are defined with an instance of the
[ sp_runtime_interface::runtime_interface](https://docs.rs/sp-runtime-interface-proc-macro/21.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sp_runtime_interface_proc_macro/attr.runtime_interface.html) macro.

Most notably, this crate contains host functions for:

All of the default host functions provided by this crate, and by default contained in all
substrate-based clients are amalgamated in [ SubstrateHostFunctions](https://docs.rs/type.SubstrateHostFunctions.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#externalities)Externalities

Host functions go hand in hand with the concept of externalities. Externalities are an environment in which host functions are provided, and thus can be accessed. Some host functions are only accessible in an externality environment that provides it.

A typical error for substrate developers is the following:

This code will panic with the following error:

`thread 'main' panicked at '`get_version_1` called outside of an Externalities-provided environment.'`Such error messages should always be interpreted as “code accessing host functions accessed outside of externalities”.

An externality is any type that implements [ sp_externalities::Externalities](https://docs.rs/sp-externalities/0.34.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sp_externalities/trait.Externalities.html). A simple example
of which is

[, which is commonly used in tests and is exported from this crate.](https://docs.rs/type.TestExternalities.html)

`TestExternalities````
use sp_io::{storage::get, TestExternalities};
TestExternalities::default().execute_with(|| {
	let data = get(b"hello world");
});
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [allocator](https://docs.rs/allocator/index.html)
- Wasm only interface that provides functions for calling into the allocator.
- [crypto](https://docs.rs/crypto/index.html)
- Interfaces for working with crypto related types from within the runtime.
- [default_](https://docs.rs/default_child_storage/index.html)- child_ - storage
- Interface for accessing the child storage for default child trie, from within the runtime.
- [hashing](https://docs.rs/hashing/index.html)
- Interface that provides functions for hashing with different algorithms.
- [logging](https://docs.rs/logging/index.html)
- Interface that provides functions for logging from within the runtime.
- [misc](https://docs.rs/misc/index.html)
- Interface that provides miscellaneous functions for communicating between the runtime and the node.
- [offchain](https://docs.rs/offchain/index.html)
- Interface that provides functions to access the offchain functionality.
- [offchain_](https://docs.rs/offchain_index/index.html)- index
- Interface that provides functions to access the Offchain DB.
- [panic_](https://docs.rs/panic_handler/index.html)- handler
- WASM-only interface which allows for aborting the execution in case of an unrecoverable error.
- [storage](https://docs.rs/storage/index.html)
- Interface for accessing the storage from within the runtime.
- [transaction_](https://docs.rs/transaction_index/index.html)- index
- Interface that provides transaction indexing API.
- [trie](https://docs.rs/trie/index.html)
- Interface that provides trie related functionality.
- [wasm_](https://docs.rs/wasm_tracing/index.html)- tracing
- Interface to provide tracing facilities for wasm. Modelled after tokios `tracing`-crate interfaces. See`sp-tracing`for more information.

[428](#428)		value_out: PassFatPointerAndReadWrite<&mut [u8]>,

[430](#430)	) -> AllocateAndReturnByCodec<Option<u32>> {
[431](#431)		let child_info = ChildInfo::new_default(storage_key);
[432](#432)		self.child_storage(&child_info, key).map(|value| {

[434](#434)			let data = &value[value_offset.min(value.len())..];
[435](#435)			let written = core::cmp::min(data.len(), value_out.len());
[436](#436)			value_out[..written].copy_from_slice(&data[..written]);
[437](#437)			data.len() as u32
[438](#438)		})
[439](#439)	}

[924](#924)	fn ed25519_verify(
[928](#928)		sig: PassPointerAndRead<&ed25519::Signature, 64>,
[929](#929)		msg: PassFatPointerAndRead<&[u8]>,
[930](#930)		pub_key: PassPointerAndRead<&ed25519::Public, 32>,
[931](#931)	) -> bool {
[932](#932)		if sp_externalities::with_externalities(|mut e| e.extension::<UseDalekExt>().is_some())
[936](#936)			.unwrap_or_default()
[937](#937)		{
[938](#938)			use ed25519_dalek::Verifier;
[939](#939)
[940](#940)			let Ok(public_key) = ed25519_dalek::VerifyingKey::from_bytes(&pub_key.0) else {
[941](#941)				return false;
[942](#942)			};
[943](#943)
[944](#944)			let sig = ed25519_dalek::Signature::from_bytes(&sig.0);
[945](#945)
[946](#946)			public_key.verify(msg, &sig).is_ok()
[947](#947)		} else {
[948](#948)			ed25519::Pair::verify(sig, msg, pub_key)
[949](#949)		}
[950](#950)	}

[1242](#1242)	fn secp256k1_ecdsa_recover(
[1251](#1251)		sig: PassPointerAndRead<&[u8; 65], 65>,
[1252](#1252)		msg: PassPointerAndRead<&[u8; 32], 32>,
[1253](#1253)	) -> AllocateAndReturnByCodec<Result<[u8; 64], EcdsaVerifyError>> {
[1254](#1254)		let rid = libsecp256k1::RecoveryId::parse(
[1255](#1255)			if sig[64] > 26 { sig[64] - 27 } else { sig[64] } as u8,
[1256](#1256)		)
[1257](#1257)		.map_err(|_| EcdsaVerifyError::BadV)?;
[1258](#1258)		let sig = libsecp256k1::Signature::parse_overflowing_slice(&sig[..64])
[1259](#1259)			.map_err(|_| EcdsaVerifyError::BadRS)?;
[1260](#1260)		let msg = libsecp256k1::Message::parse(msg);
[1261](#1261)		let pubkey =
[1262](#1262)			libsecp256k1::recover(&msg, &sig, &rid).map_err(|_| EcdsaVerifyError::BadSignature)?;
[1263](#1263)		let mut res = [0u8; 64];
[1264](#1264)		res.copy_from_slice(&pubkey.serialize()[1..65]);
[1265](#1265)		Ok(res)
[1266](#1266)	}
[1267](#1267)
[1268](#1268)	#[version(2)]
[1276](#1276)	fn secp256k1_ecdsa_recover(
[1277](#1277)		sig: PassPointerAndRead<&[u8; 65], 65>,
[1278](#1278)		msg: PassPointerAndRead<&[u8; 32], 32>,
[1279](#1279)	) -> AllocateAndReturnByCodec<Result<[u8; 64], EcdsaVerifyError>> {
[1280](#1280)		let rid = RecoveryId::from_i32(if sig[64] > 26 { sig[64] - 27 } else { sig[64] } as i32)
[1281](#1281)			.map_err(|_| EcdsaVerifyError::BadV)?;
[1282](#1282)		let sig = RecoverableSignature::from_compact(&sig[..64], rid)
[1283](#1283)			.map_err(|_| EcdsaVerifyError::BadRS)?;
[1284](#1284)		let msg = Message::from_digest_slice(msg).expect("Message is 32 bytes; qed");
[1285](#1285)		#[cfg(feature = "std")]
[1286](#1286)		let ctx = secp256k1::SECP256K1;
[1287](#1287)		#[cfg(not(feature = "std"))]
[1288](#1288)		let ctx = secp256k1::Secp256k1::<secp256k1::VerifyOnly>::gen_new();
[1289](#1289)		let pubkey = ctx.recover_ecdsa(&msg, &sig).map_err(|_| EcdsaVerifyError::BadSignature)?;
[1290](#1290)		let mut res = [0u8; 64];
[1291](#1291)		res.copy_from_slice(&pubkey.serialize_uncompressed()[1..]);
[1292](#1292)		Ok(res)
[1293](#1293)	}

[1815](#1815)#[runtime_interface(wasm_only, no_tracing)]
[1818](#1818)pub trait WasmTracing {
[1819](#1819)	fn enabled(&mut self, metadata: PassFatPointerAndDecode<sp_tracing::WasmMetadata>) -> bool {
[1829](#1829)		let metadata: &tracing_core::metadata::Metadata<'static> = (&metadata).into();
[1830](#1830)		tracing::dispatcher::get_default(|d| d.enabled(metadata))
[1831](#1831)	}
[1832](#1832)
[1833](#1833)	fn enter_span(
[1840](#1840)		&mut self,
[1841](#1841)		span: PassFatPointerAndDecode<sp_tracing::WasmEntryAttributes>,
[1842](#1842)	) -> u64 {
[1843](#1843)		let span: tracing::Span = span.into();
[1844](#1844)		match span.id() {
[1845](#1845)			Some(id) => tracing::dispatcher::get_default(|d| {
[1846](#1846)				let final_id = d.clone_span(&id);
[1849](#1849)				d.enter(&final_id);
[1850](#1850)				final_id.into_u64()
[1851](#1851)			}),
[1852](#1852)			_ => 0,
[1853](#1853)		}
[1854](#1854)	}
[1855](#1855)
[1856](#1856)	fn event(&mut self, event: PassFatPointerAndDecode<sp_tracing::WasmEntryAttributes>) {
[1858](#1858)		event.emit();
[1859](#1859)	}
[1860](#1860)
[1861](#1861)	fn exit(&mut self, span: u64) {
[1864](#1864)		tracing::dispatcher::get_default(|d| {
[1865](#1865)			let id = tracing_core::span::Id::from_u64(span);
[1866](#1866)			d.exit(&id);
[1867](#1867)		});
[1868](#1868)	}

- [ecdsa_](https://docs.rs/fn.ecdsa_sign.html)- sign

- [ecdsa_](https://docs.rs/fn.ecdsa_sign_prehashed.html)- sign_ - prehashed

- [ecdsa_](https://docs.rs/fn.ecdsa_verify.html)- verify

- [ecdsa_](https://docs.rs/fn.ecdsa_verify_prehashed.html)- verify_ - prehashed

- [ed25519_](https://docs.rs/fn.ed25519_generate.html)- generate

- [ed25519_](https://docs.rs/fn.ed25519_verify.html)- verify

- [secp256k1_](https://docs.rs/fn.secp256k1_ecdsa_recover.html)- ecdsa_ - recover
- Verify and recover a SECP256k1 ECDSA signature.
- [secp256k1_](https://docs.rs/fn.secp256k1_ecdsa_recover_compressed.html)- ecdsa_ - recover_ - compressed
- Verify and recover a SECP256k1 ECDSA signature.
- [sr25519_](https://docs.rs/fn.sr25519_generate.html)- generate

# sp_io::storage - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sp-io/48.0.0/sp_io/storage/index.html

## Expand description

Interface for accessing the storage from within the runtime.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Host](https://docs.rs/struct.HostFunctions.html)- Functions
- Provides implementations for the extern host functions.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [append](https://docs.rs/fn.append.html)
- Append the encoded `value`to the storage item at`key`.
- [changes_](https://docs.rs/fn.changes_root.html)- root
- Always returns `None`. This function exists for compatibility reasons.
- [clear](https://docs.rs/fn.clear.html)
- Clear the storage of the given `key`and its value.
- [clear_](https://docs.rs/fn.clear_prefix.html)- prefix
- Clear the storage of each key-value pair where the key starts with the given `prefix`.
- [commit_](https://docs.rs/fn.commit_transaction.html)- transaction
- Commit the last transaction started by `start_transaction`.
- [exists](https://docs.rs/fn.exists.html)
- Check whether the given `key`exists in storage.
- [get](https://docs.rs/fn.get.html)
- Returns the data for `key`in the storage or`None`if the key can not be found.
- [next_](https://docs.rs/fn.next_key.html)- key
- Get the next key in storage after the given one in lexicographic order.
- [read](https://docs.rs/fn.read.html)
- Get `key`from storage, placing the value into`value_out`and return the number of bytes that the entry in storage has beyond the offset or`None`if the storage entry doesn’t exist at all. If`value_out`length is smaller than the returned length, only`value_out`length bytes are copied into`value_out`.
- [rollback_](https://docs.rs/fn.rollback_transaction.html)- transaction
- Rollback the last transaction started by `start_transaction`.
- [root](https://docs.rs/fn.root.html)
- “Commit” all existing operations and compute the resulting storage root.
- [set](https://docs.rs/fn.set.html)
- Set `key`to`value`in the storage.
- [start_](https://docs.rs/fn.start_transaction.html)- transaction
- Start a new nested transaction.

# UseDalekExt in sp_io - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sp-io/48.0.0/sp_io/struct.UseDalekExt.html

`pub struct UseDalekExt;`## Expand description

Extension to signal to [`crypt::ed25519_verify`] to use the dalek crate.

The switch from `ed25519-dalek` to `ed25519-zebra` was a breaking change.
`ed25519-zebra` is more permissive when it comes to the verification of signatures.
This means that some chains may fail to sync from genesis when using `ed25519-zebra`.
So, this extension can be registered to the runtime execution environment to signal
that `ed25519-dalek` should be used for verification. The extension can be registered
in the following way:

```
client.execution_extensions().set_extensions_factory(
	// Let the `UseDalekExt` extension being registered for each runtime invocation
	// until the execution happens in the context of block `1000`.
	sc_client_api::execution_extensions::ExtensionBeforeBlock::<Block, UseDalekExt>::new(1000)
);
```

# KillStorageResult in sp_io - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sp-io/48.0.0/sp_io/enum.KillStorageResult.html

## Expand description

The outcome of calling `storage_kill`. Returned value is the number of storage items
removed from the backend from making the `storage_kill` call.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.AllRemoved)

### AllRemoved([u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html))

All keys to remove were removed, return number of iterations performed during the operation.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.SomeRemaining)

### SomeRemaining([u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html))

Not all key to remove were removed, return number of iterations performed during the operation.

# sp_io - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sp-io/latest/sp_io/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#substrate-primitives-io)Substrate Primitives: IO

This crate contains interfaces for the runtime to communicate with the outside world, ergo `io`.
In other context, such interfaces are referred to as “**host functions**”.

Each set of host functions are defined with an instance of the
[ sp_runtime_interface::runtime_interface](https://docs.rs/sp-runtime-interface-proc-macro/21.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sp_runtime_interface_proc_macro/attr.runtime_interface.html) macro.

Most notably, this crate contains host functions for:

All of the default host functions provided by this crate, and by default contained in all
substrate-based clients are amalgamated in [ SubstrateHostFunctions](https://docs.rs/type.SubstrateHostFunctions.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#externalities)Externalities

Host functions go hand in hand with the concept of externalities. Externalities are an environment in which host functions are provided, and thus can be accessed. Some host functions are only accessible in an externality environment that provides it.

A typical error for substrate developers is the following:

This code will panic with the following error:

`thread 'main' panicked at '`get_version_1` called outside of an Externalities-provided environment.'`Such error messages should always be interpreted as “code accessing host functions accessed outside of externalities”.

An externality is any type that implements [ sp_externalities::Externalities](https://docs.rs/sp-externalities/0.34.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sp_externalities/trait.Externalities.html). A simple example
of which is

[, which is commonly used in tests and is exported from this crate.](https://docs.rs/type.TestExternalities.html)

`TestExternalities````
use sp_io::{storage::get, TestExternalities};
TestExternalities::default().execute_with(|| {
	let data = get(b"hello world");
});
```

# bytes 1.12.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/bytes/^1.4.0

# Bytes

A utility library for working with bytes.

## Usage

To use `bytes`, first add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "1"
```
Next, add this to your crate:

```
use ;
```
## no_std support

To use `bytes` with no_std environment, disable the (enabled by default) `std` feature.

```
[]
 = {  = "1",  = false }
```
To use `bytes` with no_std environment without atomic CAS, such as thumbv6m, you also need to enable
the `extra-platforms` feature. See the [documentation for the  portable-atomic
crate](https://docs.rs/portable-atomic) for more information.

The MSRV when `extra-platforms` feature is enabled depends on the MSRV of `portable-atomic`.

## Serde support

Serde support is optional and disabled by default. To enable use the feature `serde`.

```
[]
 = {  = "1",  = ["serde"] }
```
The MSRV when `serde` feature is enabled depends on the MSRV of `serde`.

## Building documentation

When building the `bytes` documentation the `docsrs` option should be used, otherwise
feature gates will not be shown. This requires a nightly toolchain:

```
RUSTDOCFLAGS="--cfg docsrs" cargo +nightly doc
```

This project is licensed under the [MIT license](https://docs.rs/LICENSE).

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted
for inclusion in `bytes` by you, shall be licensed as MIT, without any additional
terms or conditions.

# parity-scale-codec 3.7.5 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/parity-scale-codec/^3.7.5

# Parity SCALE Codec

Rust implementation of the SCALE (Simple Concatenated Aggregate Little-Endian) data format for types used in the Parity Substrate framework.

SCALE is a light-weight format which allows encoding (and decoding) which makes it highly suitable for resource-constrained execution environments like blockchain runtimes and low-power, low-memory devices.

It is important to note that the encoding context (knowledge of how the types and data structures look) needs to be known separately at both encoding and decoding ends. The encoded data does not include this contextual information.

To get a better understanding of how the encoding is done for different types,
take a look at the ["Type encoding (SCALE)" page in Substrate docs](https://docs.substrate.io/reference/scale-codec/).

## Implementation

The codec is implemented using the following traits:

### Encode

The `Encode` trait is used for encoding of data into the SCALE format. The `Encode` trait
contains the following functions:

- `size_hint(&self) -> usize`: Gets the capacity (in bytes) required for the encoded data. This is to avoid double-allocation of memory needed for the encoding. It can be an estimate and does not need to be an exact number. If the size is not known, even no good maximum, then we can skip this function from the trait implementation. This is required to be a cheap operation, so should not involve iterations etc.
- `encode_to<T: Output>(&self, dest: &mut T)`: Encodes the value and appends it to a destination buffer.
- `encode(&self) -> Vec<u8>`: Encodes the type data and returns a slice.
- `using_encoded<R, F: FnOnce(&[u8]) -> R>(&self, f: F) -> R`: Encodes the type data and executes a closure on the encoded value. Returns the result from the executed closure.

**Note:** Implementations should override `using_encoded` for value types and `encode_to` for
allocating types. `size_hint` should be implemented for all types, wherever possible. Wrapper
types should override all methods.

### Decode

The `Decode` trait is used for deserialization/decoding of encoded data into the respective
types.

- `fn decode<I: Input>(value: &mut I) -> Result<Self, Error>`: Tries to decode the value from SCALE format to the type it is called on. Returns an- `Err`if the decoding fails.

### CompactAs

The `CompactAs` trait is used for wrapping custom types/structs as compact types, which makes
them even more space/memory efficient. The compact encoding is described [here](https://docs.substrate.io/reference/scale-codec/#fn-1).

- `encode_as(&self) -> &Self::As`: Encodes the type (self) as a compact type. The type- `As`is defined in the same trait and its implementation should be compact encode-able.
- `decode_from(_: Self::As) -> Result<Self, Error>`: Decodes the type (self) from a compact encode-able type.

### HasCompact

The `HasCompact` trait, if implemented, tells that the corresponding type is a compact
encode-able type.

### EncodeLike

The `EncodeLike` trait needs to be implemented for each type manually. When using derive, it is
done automatically for you. Basically the trait gives you the opportunity to accept multiple
types to a function that all encode to the same representation.

## Usage Examples

Following are some examples to demonstrate usage of the codec.

### Simple types

```
# // Import macros if derive feature is not used.
#
# use ;
use ;
let a = A;
let b = B;
let c = C ;
a.using_encoded;
b.using_encoded;
c.using_encoded;
let mut da: & = b"\x0f";
assert_eq!;
let mut db: & = b"\x01\x01\0\0\0\x02\0\0\0\0\0\0\0";
assert_eq!;
let mut dc: & = b"\x02\x01\0\0\0\x02\0\0\0\0\0\0\0";
assert_eq!;
let mut dz: & = &;
assert_eq!;
#
```
### Compact type with HasCompact

```
# // Import macros if derive feature is not used.
#
# use ;
use ;
let test_val:  = ;
let encoded = Test1HasCompact .encode;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
#
```
### Type with CompactAs

```
# // Import macros if derive feature is not used.
#
# use ;
use ;
use ;
;
let a =  ;
let encoded = a.encode;
assert_eq!;
#
```
## Derive attributes

The derive implementation supports the following attributes:

- `codec(dumb_trait_bound)`: This attribute needs to be placed above the type that one of the trait should be implemented for. It will make the algorithm that determines the to-add trait bounds fall back to just use the type parameters of the type. This can be useful for situation where the algorithm includes private types in the public interface. By using this attribute, you should not get this error/warning again.
- `codec(skip)`: Needs to be placed above a field or variant and makes it to be skipped while encoding/decoding.
- `codec(compact)`: Needs to be placed above a field and makes the field use compact encoding. (The type needs to support compact encoding.)
- `codec(encoded_as = "OtherType")`: Needs to be placed above a field and makes the field being encoded by using- `OtherType`.
- `codec(index = 0)`: Needs to be placed above an enum variant to make the variant use the given index when encoded. By default the index is determined by counting from- `0`beginning wth the first variant.
- `codec(encode_bound)`,- `codec(decode_bound)`and- `codec(mel_bound)`: All 3 attributes take in a- `where`clause for the- `Encode`,- `Decode`and- `MaxEncodedLen`trait implementation for the annotated type respectively.
- `codec(encode_bound(skip_type_params))`,- `codec(decode_bound(skip_type_params))`and- `codec(mel_bound(skip_type_params))`: All 3 sub-attributes take in types as arguments to skip trait derivation of the corresponding trait, e.g. T in- `codec(encode_bound(skip_type_params(T)))`will not contain a- `Encode`trait bound while- `Encode`is being derived for the annotated type.

## Known issues

Even though this crate supports deserialization of arbitrarily sized array (e.g. `[T; 1024 * 1024 * 1024]`)
using such types is not recommended and will most likely result in a stack overflow. If you have a big
array inside of your structure which you want to decode you should wrap it in a `Box`, e.g. `Box<[T; 1024 * 1024 * 1024]>`.

# secp256k1 0.28.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/secp256k1/^0.28.0

`rust-secp256k1` is a wrapper around [libsecp256k1](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/secp256k1), a C
library implementing various cryptographic functions using the [SECG](https://www.secg.org/) curve
[secp256k1](https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Secp256k1).

This library:

- exposes type-safe Rust bindings for all `libsecp256k1`functions
- implements key generation
- implements deterministic nonce generation via RFC6979
- implements many unit tests, adding to those already present in `libsecp256k1`
- makes no allocations (except in unit tests) for efficiency and use in freestanding implementations

### Contributing

Contributions to this library are welcome. A few guidelines:

- Any breaking changes must have an accompanied entry in CHANGELOG.md
- No new dependencies, please.
- No crypto should be implemented in Rust, with the possible exception of hash functions. Cryptographic contributions should be directed upstream to libsecp256k1.
- This library should always compile with any combination of features on **Rust 1.48.0**.

### Githooks

To assist devs in catching errors *before* running CI we provide some githooks. If you do not
already have locally configured githooks you can use the ones in this repository by running, in the
root directory of the repository:

```
git config --local core.hooksPath githooks/
```
Alternatively add symlinks in your `.git/hooks` directory to any of the githooks we provide.

### Benchmarks

We use a custom Rust compiler configuration conditional to guard the bench mark code. To run the
bench marks use: `RUSTFLAGS='--cfg=bench' cargo +nightly bench --features=recovery`.

### A note on `non_secure_erase`

This crate's secret types (`SecretKey`, `Keypair`, `SharedSecret`, `Scalar`, and `DisplaySecret`)
have a method called `non_secure_erase` that *attempts* to overwrite the contained secret. This
method is provided to assist other libraries in building secure secret erasure. However, this
library makes no guarantees about the security of using `non_secure_erase`. In particular,
the compiler doesn't have any concept of secrets and in most cases can arbitrarily move or copy
values anywhere it pleases. For more information, consult the [ zeroize](https://docs.rs/zeroize)
documentation.

## Fuzzing

If you want to fuzz this library, or any library which depends on it, you will
probably want to disable the actual cryptography, since fuzzers are unable to
forge signatures and therefore won't test many interesting codepaths. To instead
use a trivially-broken but fuzzer-accessible signature scheme, compile with
`--cfg=secp256k1_fuzz` in your `RUSTFLAGS` variable.

Note that `cargo hfuzz` does **not** set this config flag automatically. In 0.27.0
and earlier versions, we used the `--cfg=fuzzing` which honggfuzz does set, but we
changed this because there was no way to override it.

# sp-runtime-interface 37.0.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sp-runtime-interface/^37.0.0

Substrate runtime interface

This crate provides types, traits and macros around runtime interfaces. A runtime interface is a fixed interface between a Substrate runtime and a Substrate node. For a native runtime the interface maps to a direct function call of the implementation. For a wasm runtime the interface maps to an external function call. These external functions are exported by the wasm executor and they map to the same implementation as the native calls.

# Using a type in a runtime interface

Any type that should be used in a runtime interface as argument or return value needs to implement [`RIType`]. The
associated type
[ FFIType](https://docs.rs/docs.rs/sp-runtime-interface/latest/sp_runtime_interface/trait.RIType.html#associatedtype.FFIType) is
the type that is used in the FFI function to represent the actual type. For example

`[T]` is represented by an `u64`.
The slice pointer and the length will be mapped to an `u64` value. For more information see this
[table](https://docs.rs/docs.rs/sp-runtime-interface/latest/sp_runtime_interface/#ffi-type-and-conversion). The FFI function definition is used when calling from the wasm runtime into the node.

Traits are used to convert from a type to the corresponding
[ RIType::FFIType](https://docs.rs/docs.rs/sp-runtime-interface/latest/sp_runtime_interface/trait.RIType.html#associatedtype.FFIType).
Depending on where and how a type should be used in a function signature, a combination of the following traits need to
be implemented:

- Pass as function argument: [`wasm::IntoFFIValue`] and [`host::FromFFIValue`]
- As function return value: [`wasm::FromFFIValue`] and [`host::IntoFFIValue`]
- Pass as mutable function argument: [`host::IntoPreallocatedFFIValue`]

The traits are implemented for most of the common types like `[T]`, `Vec<T>`, arrays and primitive types.

For custom types, we provide the
[ PassBy](https://docs.rs/sp-runtime-interface/latest/sp_runtime_interface/pass_by#PassBy) trait and strategies that
define how a type is passed between the wasm runtime and the node. Each strategy also provides a derive macro to
simplify the implementation.

# Performance

To not waste any more performance when calling into the node, not all types are SCALE encoded when being passed as
arguments between the wasm runtime and the node. For most types that are raw bytes like `Vec<u8>`, `[u8]` or `[u8; N]`
we pass them directly, without SCALE encoding them in front of. The implementation of [`RIType`] each type provides more
information on how the data is passed.

# Declaring a runtime interface

Declaring a runtime interface is similar to declaring a trait in Rust:

```
```
For more information on declaring a runtime interface, see
[ #[runtime_interface]](https://docs.rs/sp-runtime-interface/latest/sp_runtime_interface/attr.runtime_interface.html).

# FFI type and conversion

The following table documents how values of types are passed between the wasm and the host side and how they are converted into the corresponding type.

| Type | FFI type | Conversion |
|---|---|---|
| `u8` | `u8` | `Identity` |
| `u16` | `u16` | `Identity` |
| `u32` | `u32` | `Identity` |
| `u64` | `u64` | `Identity` |
| `i128` | `u32` | `v.as_ptr()`(pointer to a 16 byte array) |
| `i8` | `i8` | `Identity` |
| `i16` | `i16` | `Identity` |
| `i32` | `i32` | `Identity` |
| `i64` | `i64` | `Identity` |
| `u128` | `u32` | `v.as_ptr()`(pointer to a 16 byte array) |
| `bool` | `u8` | `if v { 1 } else { 0 }` |
| `&str` | `u64` | v.len() 32bit << 32 | v.as_ptr() 32bit |
| `&[u8]` | `u64` | v.len() 32bit << 32 | v.as_ptr() 32bit |
| `Vec<u8>` | `u64` | v.len() 32bit << 32 | v.as_ptr() 32bit |
| `Vec<T> where T: Encode` | `u64` | `let e = v.encode();`e.len() 32bit << 32 | e.as_ptr() 32bit |
| `&[T] where T: Encode` | `u64` | `let e = v.encode();`e.len() 32bit << 32 | e.as_ptr() 32bit |
| `[u8; N]` | `u32` | `v.as_ptr()` |
| `*const T` | `u32` | `Identity` |
| `Option<T>` | `u64` | `let e = v.encode();`e.len() 32bit << 32 | e.as_ptr() 32bit |
| `T where T: PassBy<PassBy=Inner>` | Depends on inner | Depends on inner |
| `T where T: PassBy<PassBy=Codec>` | `u64` | v.len() 32bit << 32 | v.as_ptr() 32bit |

`Identity` means that the value is converted directly into the corresponding FFI type.

# sp-tracing 19.0.0 - Docs.rs

Substrate tracing primitives and macros.

To trace functions or individual code in Substrate, this crate provides [`within_span`]
and [`enter_span`]. See the individual docs for how to use these macros.

Note that to allow traces from wasm execution environment there are
2 reserved identifiers for tracing `Field` recording, stored in the consts:
`WASM_TARGET_KEY` and `WASM_NAME_KEY` - if you choose to record fields, you
must ensure that your identifiers do not clash with either of these.

Additionally, we have a const: `WASM_TRACE_IDENTIFIER`, which holds a span name used
to signal that the 'actual' span name and target should be retrieved instead from
the associated Fields mentioned above.
